counterexample: Take the diamond lattice M3: the set {0, a, b, c, 1} ordered so that 0 < a, b, c < 1 with a, b, c pairwise incomparable. M3 is a finite lattice, hence a complete lattice (every subset has a join and a meet), so M3 is an object of CLat. But M3 is not a frame: the frame (infinite) distributive law a AND (join of S) = join of {a AND s : s in S} fails already for the two-element set S = {b, c}, since a AND (b OR c) = a AND 1 = a, whereas (a AND b) OR (a AND c) = 0 OR 0 = 0, and a != 0. Hence M3 is an object of CLat that is not an object of Frm, so the objects of CLat are NOT a subcollection of the objects of Frm, contradicting line 0002 (and therefore the subcategory conclusion of line 0009).
reasoning_summary: The proof's load-bearing claim is line 0002: that CLat consists of a subcollection of the objects and a subcollection of the morphisms of Frm. The only authority cited for it is 'Complete Lattice Homomorphism is Frame Homomorphism', which is a statement about morphisms (and presupposes that its domain/codomain are frames); it says nothing about objects. In fact the object inclusion runs the wrong way: frames are by definition complete lattices satisfying the infinite distributive law, so every frame is a complete lattice, but not conversely. M3 (0 < a,b,c < 1, with a,b,c pairwise incomparable) is a finite hence complete lattice with a AND (b OR c) = a but (a AND b) OR (a AND c) = 0, so it is a complete lattice that is not a frame. Thus CLat has objects Frm does not have, line 0002 is false under the stated definitions, and the conclusion at line 0009 does not follow (indeed the theorem as stated fails: the containment of object collections is the reverse, while the morphism containment goes the stated way only after restricting to frames).
counterexample_target: line 0002 (objects of CLat form a subcollection of objects of Frm)
